understanding.core_idea: Paging removes the requirement for contiguity, so scattered free frames become usable and external fragmentation disappears.

script.question: Why does an operating system use paging instead of contiguous allocation?

beats.speaker: interviewer
beats.line: Why does an operating system use paging instead of contiguous allocation?

beats.speaker: student
beats.line: Contiguous allocation forces every single process to occupy one unbroken block of physical memory.
beats.source_quote: Contiguous allocation forces every process to occupy one unbroken block of physical memory.

beats.speaker: student
beats.line: Over time that produces external fragmentation: enough total free memory exists, but no single block is large enough.
beats.source_quote: Over time this produces external fragmentation: enough total free memory exists, but no single block is large enough.

beats.speaker: student
beats.line: Paging removes that requirement for contiguity, and that single change is what fixes the problem.
beats.source_quote: Paging removes the requirement for contiguity.

beats.speaker: student
beats.line: Memory is divided into fixed-size frames and the logical address space into pages of the same size.
beats.source_quote: Physical memory is divided into fixed-size frames and the logical address space is divided into pages of the same size.

beats.speaker: student
beats.line: So any page may be placed in any free frame, which makes the scattered gaps usable.
beats.source_quote: Any page may be placed in any free frame.
